title: Intention Before Action
principle: Karma begins with intention. Before an action becomes a result, it is a choice about what we place into the world.
image: Imagine a single seed resting in dark soil. It does not rush toward the light. It receives water, warmth, and time, then responds.
inquiry: Notice one intention beneath today’s effort. It may be to contribute, to learn, or to care. Let the intention become simple and honest.
action: Choose one small action that matches your intention. A thoughtful reply. A patient beginning. A promise kept without needing recognition.

title: Trust the Season
principle: Patience is active steadiness. It lets wise action ripen without demanding that every result arrive now.
image: Picture bamboo moving in a light wind. It bends, returns, and keeps growing through seasons that cannot be hurried.
inquiry: Bring to mind one result you have been pressing toward. Feel the energy of that effort, then loosen your grip around the timetable.
action: Choose the next faithful step and let it be enough. Progress can be quiet. A path still unfolds when you walk it without strain.

title: The Clear Pause
principle: Deliberation creates space between impulse and action. In that space, what matters can become easier to see.
image: Imagine a cup of cloudy water resting on a table. Left undisturbed, the sediment settles and the water becomes clear by itself.
inquiry: Notice a decision asking for your attention. You do not need to solve it now. Let the facts, feelings, and values rest beside one another.
action: Carry one clear question into the day: what choice creates the least unnecessary force? Let your answer arrive at a human pace.

title: Beginner’s Mind
principle: A beginner’s mind meets experience before naming it. Curiosity opens paths that certainty can overlook.
image: Picture a mountain trail disappearing into morning mist. You cannot see the whole route, yet the next stone is visible beneath your feet.
inquiry: Notice where certainty has become tight. Allow one familiar problem to become new again. What have you not yet asked or noticed?
action: Take one curious step today. Listen before concluding. Try a smaller experiment. Let discovery matter more than appearing certain.

title: A Steady Center
principle: Equanimity is a balanced heart. It makes room for difficulty and delight without being carried away by either one.
image: Imagine a mountain reflected in changing water. Wind alters the reflection, while the mountain remains grounded beneath the open sky.
inquiry: Notice what is pulling you forward or pushing you away. Name it gently, without making it an enemy or a command.
action: Meet one changing moment with a steady response. Pause, feel your feet, and choose the action that respects the whole situation.

title: Open Hands
principle: Non-attachment means caring fully without trying to possess every outcome. Effort can be sincere while the hands remain open.
image: Picture an autumn leaf carried along a clear stream. The water holds it for a while, then lets it continue around the bend.
inquiry: Bring to mind one outcome you are holding tightly. Keep the care, the skill, and the effort. Soften the demand for certainty.
action: Do the work that belongs to you, then release the part that does not. Leave a little room for life to answer in its own way.

title: Effort Without Strain
principle: Right effort is energy guided by wisdom. It supports what is helpful and stops feeding what leaves the mind depleted.
image: Imagine a gardener tending a small courtyard. Water goes where it is needed. Weeds are removed gently. Growth is invited, not forced.
inquiry: Notice where effort feels clean and where it feels contracted. Your body often knows the difference before your thoughts explain it.
action: Give today’s best energy to one meaningful task. Let one unnecessary struggle wait. Sustainable effort is a form of respect.

title: Strength with Warmth
principle: Compassion joins clear seeing with the wish to reduce suffering. It is warmth with boundaries, courage, and practical action.
image: Picture a lantern beside a dark path. It does not light the whole journey. It offers enough warmth and clarity for the next few steps.
inquiry: Notice the person within you who has been working hard. Speak inwardly with the same steadiness you would offer a trusted friend.
action: Let one choice today combine strength with warmth. Be direct without becoming hard. Be kind without abandoning what matters.

title: Still Water
principle: Stillness is not the absence of movement. It is what a surface does on its own once nothing new is thrown into it. You need only stop stirring.
image: Picture a lake at first light, before any wind. Mountains stand in it, inverted and clear. The water is not holding that picture; it is simply not disturbing it.
inquiry: Find where you are still stirring something. A conversation rehearsed, a decision turned over. Set the stick down and let the water answer for itself.
action: Leave one thing undisturbed today. A pause before you reply. A breath before you open the door. Let stillness be something you allow rather than achieve.

title: One Thing at a Time
principle: Focus is not a reserve you spend until it runs dry. It is a place you stand, and you can only stand in one place. Choosing where is most of the work.
image: Think of a brush held above paper. Before the stroke the whole hand is quiet. The line is good because nothing else was being attempted alongside it.
inquiry: Notice how many things are asking for you at once. Let each one call from where it is. You do not have to travel to any of them for these few minutes.
action: Give one thing your whole attention today. One meal, one conversation, one page. Let the others wait where they are without apology.

title: The Small Corrections
principle: Balance is not a posture held perfectly. Anyone standing still is correcting constantly. The corrections are not failures of balance; they are the balance.
image: Picture a heron in shallow water, resting on one leg. It appears entirely still, and it is adjusting without pause. That is precisely why it stays up.
inquiry: Feel your weight shift a little with each breath, and let it. Notice where you have been holding something rigid in the hope that it would stop moving.
action: Make one small correction today rather than one large repair. Ten minutes earlier. One thing declined. Something set down before it grew heavy.

title: A Reason to Rise
principle: Ikigai is often described as a grand purpose. It is smaller than that. It is the specific, ordinary reason you got up today, and it may be very small.
image: It might be someone who would notice your absence. A plant that needs water. Work left half done. Bread you wanted to eat while it was still warm.
inquiry: Let one of those come to mind. Do not weigh it or rank it. Notice only where you feel it in the body when you think of it, and breathe there a while.
action: Give that reason ten minutes before the day fills up. Not the whole of it. Ten minutes, early, while it still belongs to you.

title: The Golden Seam
principle: Kintsugi repairs broken pottery with gold. The crack is not concealed or made to look new. It is filled and traced, and becomes the most looked at part of the bowl.
image: Picture the seam: a thin gold river running across the glaze. You can see exactly where it broke. The bowl is not pretending, and it still holds water.
inquiry: Bring attention to something in you that healed. Do not open it. Let it simply be there, breathing, without being called damage.
action: Let one repaired thing be visible today. An apology already made. A habit already changed. Let it count rather than hiding it.

title: The Unfinished Bowl
principle: Wabi-sabi finds beauty in what is worn, uneven and unfinished. Not in spite of those qualities, but because of them. Nothing becomes lovely by becoming perfect.
image: A tea bowl thrown slightly off centre, glazed unevenly, its rim a little low on one side. It has been used for two hundred years, and that is why it is treasured.
inquiry: Find something in yourself you have been treating as a draft of someone better. Let it be finished as it is, at least for the length of this breath.
action: Let one imperfect thing stand today. The crooked shelf. The reply that was good enough. The day that went sideways and still ended.

title: The Petal Falling
principle: Mono no aware is the quiet ache at the heart of lovely things, because they do not stay. It is not grief. It is the tenderness that comes with paying attention.
image: Blossom coming off a branch in a light wind. Nobody watching wishes it were plastic. The falling is not the flaw in the flower; it is the whole of it.
inquiry: Rest on the breath you are in. It is leaving as you hold it. You are not losing it. You are being present for it while it is here.
action: Let one ordinary thing register today as though it were rare. A face across a table. Light on a wall at a particular hour.

title: The Space Between
principle: Ma is the interval. Not empty space, but the space that gives everything else its shape. A room is useful because of the part with nothing in it.
image: Ink on paper with wide margins left bare. The painter did not run out of paper. The emptiness is where the mountain gets to be far away.
inquiry: Return to the pause at the end of your out-breath. Do not stretch it or hurry it. Be in the interval rather than racing toward the next thing.
action: Leave one gap on purpose today. Five minutes between two meetings. A walk taken slowly. Silence after a question instead of a quick answer.

title: More Than Is Shown
principle: Yugen is the sense that there is more than what is being shown. Not a secret to be solved, but a depth felt at the edge of a thing without reaching its end.
image: Mountains going back into mist, ridge behind ridge, until you cannot say how far it runs. The mist is not hiding the view. The mist is the view.
inquiry: Let attention go to the edge of what you can feel, where sensation turns vague. Stay there without trying to bring it into focus.
action: Let one thing stay unexplained today. A mood you do not account for. A piece of music you do not analyse. Let it keep its depth.

title: Once, and Only Now
principle: Ichigo ichie comes from the tea room: one meeting, one chance. Even with the same people in the same room, the gathering is new, because nothing has been here twice.
image: A host preparing a bowl of tea as though it were the only one, because for that guest, on that afternoon, in that light, it is.
inquiry: Come back to this breath. Not breathing in general. This one, with whatever mood you brought to it. It is the only version there will be.
action: Treat one ordinary meeting as unrepeatable today. The same colleague. The same walk home. It is the same in name only.

title: Each in Its Season
principle: Oubaitori names four trees: cherry, plum, peach and apricot. Each blossoms in its own season, in its own way. None of them is late. The comparison does not apply.
image: A plum opening in cold air while the cherry stands bare beside it. The cherry is not failing. It is doing what it does, at the hour it does it.
inquiry: Notice if some part of you is running a comparison right now, even about how this is going. Let the measuring stop for a moment and just breathe.
action: Notice one comparison today and set it down. Someone further along. Someone younger. Let them be in their season and stay in yours.

title: Without Watching Yourself
principle: Mushin is no-mind: acting without the commentary that watches you act. Not blankness, but the quiet that arrives when self-consciousness stops narrating.
image: A hand catching something falling, before the thought arrives. It was not faster thinking. It was the absence of thinking getting in the way.
inquiry: Notice the voice describing this practice while you do it. Do not argue with it. Let attention sit with the breath instead of the commentary.
action: Do one thing today without narrating it. Wash up. Walk somewhere. Let the commentary idle and the hands get on with it.

title: After the Arrow
principle: Zanshin is remaining mind: the attention that stays after the act is finished. In archery the posture is held after the arrow has gone. The shot is not over at release.
image: The archer, bow still open, eyes still down the range, long after the arrow has landed. Nothing is being achieved. The form is simply being completed.
inquiry: Finish this breath all the way out before taking the next. Let the ending be as attended as the beginning. Most of us leave early.
action: Finish one thing properly today. Close the conversation rather than drifting out of it. Put the tool back. Stay for the last minute of something.

title: Among the Trees
principle: Shinrin yoku is not a walk with a destination. It is letting the senses take in a place without turning any of it into a task. Nothing is covered or achieved.
image: Standing among tall trees with the light coming down in pieces. Bark, damp earth, movement somewhere in the branches. You are not studying it; you are in it.
inquiry: Let one sense lead for a moment. Sound, probably, with the eyes closed. Let it arrive without naming it or deciding what it means.
action: Give five minutes to your senses today. Outside if you can, a window if you cannot. Look without photographing, listen without naming.

title: Room Left Over
principle: Yutori is margin kept on purpose: the time, space or energy you deliberately do not spend. Not what is left over at the end, but what you set aside first.
image: A train timetable built with slack in it. The slack looks like waste until one train runs late, and then it is the only reason the day does not fall over.
inquiry: Let your breathing stay a little short of full. Not restricted, just unhurried. Notice that leaving room feels different from running out of it.
action: Keep some margin back today. Leave earlier than you need to. End one thing before you are empty. Let something be under-filled on purpose.
